MemTensor releases bundled a credential-stealing Go payload

Target: MemTensor · repo
Date: 2026-09-23
Target Kind: project_organization
Language: Go
Impact: credential_theft
Phase: source

Synopsis

An attacker published modified MemTensor packages to npm and PyPI. Bundled Go binaries ran during plugin use or Python import and searched developer home directories for secrets.

Story

An AI memory plugin began passing user prompts to a hidden executable on September 23, when compromised MemTensor releases introduced a program for collecting developer secrets. Socket and StepSecurity identified malicious versions of the MemOS Cloud integration for OpenClaw, alongside the Python package MemoryOS. The affected software belonged to an established project that helped AI applications retain information between interactions; the attacker inserted the collection machinery into that ordinary work.

The npm releases, 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25 of @memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin, carried executables for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Inspection of the retained 0.1.23 and 0.1.25 archives confirmed the package identities and six bundled platform binaries. StepSecurity found that gateway startup and memory recall launched the program in a detached process. During recall, the launcher also supplied the user's prompt. Disabling package-install scripts would not prevent that later execution inside the running plugin.

The payload, named sckit, targeted credentials that could unlock cloud services, source repositories, and package registries. Socket's analysis connected its collection to skyleen.fr and described the Python counterpart in MemoryOS 2.0.34, where importing memos reached the launcher through logging initialization. These entry points put the malware inside processes already entrusted with application configuration and user input. Public reporting established the malicious releases, but did not establish how the attacker first obtained access.

The release sequence complicated recovery. StepSecurity found that versions 0.1.22 and 0.1.24 restored clean contents, only for another malicious version to appear less than four minutes after each. A newer version number therefore offered no assurance that the intrusion had ended. The reports identified affected releases and collection capabilities, but supplied neither a confirmed victim count nor evidence that the successive clean-content publications had permanently removed the attacker's access.
